title: 2 Chronicles 35:20–27
context: When Neco king of Egypt goes up to fight at Carchemish, Josiah goes out against him; Neco warns that God has commanded him to hurry and that Josiah should not oppose God, but Josiah disguises himself, does not listen to “the words of Neco from the mouth of God,” and is mortally wounded at Megiddo. All Judah mourns, and Jeremiah laments for him. Neco’s warning (35:21–22) is material that 2 Kings 23:29–30 does not have; both traditions read the account as given, without inventing a hidden sin.

verses.text: After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco king of Egypt went up to fight against Carchemish by the Euphrates, and Josiah went out against him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco king of Egypt went up to fight against Carchemish by the Euphrates, and Josiah went out against him.” Arminian readers note that the narrative moves directly from faithful worship to a fatal decision.

Josiah’s reason for going out is not stated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the abrupt transition and the unstated motive.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both read the account with care rather than supplying reasons the text does not give, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 23:29.

verses.text: But he sent ambassadors to him, saying, “What have I to do with you, you king of Judah? I come not against you today, but against the house with which I have war. God has commanded me to make haste. Beware that it is God who is with me, that he not destroy you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Neco sends word: “I come not against you today... God has commanded me to make haste. Beware that it is God who is with me, that he not destroy you.” Arminian readers note that this warning is not found in 2 Kings 23:29–30.

The Chronicler presents God speaking through an unexpected messenger.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the material unique to Chronicles and the claim that God directed Neco.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God can speak through a foreign king, and the text gives the warning without explaining how Josiah should have recognized it.

verses.text: Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and didn’t listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself... and didn’t listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God.” Arminian readers note that the narrator judges Josiah’s refusal, without adding other faults.

The disguise may recall Ahab’s at Ramoth Gilead (1 Kings 22:30).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse as the Chronicler’s explanation of Josiah’s death and decline to go beyond it.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: even a faithful king can fail to heed God’s word, and the text does not suggest any hidden sin.

verses.text: The archers shot at King Josiah; and the king said to his servants, “Take me away, because I am seriously wounded!”
verses.arminianNotes:
“The archers shot at King Josiah,” and he tells his servants, “Take me away, because I am seriously wounded!” Arminian readers read the wounding soberly.

The narrative is brief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the restraint of the account.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the death of a faithful king is a grief, and the text reports it without elaboration.

verses.text: So his servants took him out of the chariot, and put him in the second chariot that he had, and brought him to Jerusalem; and he died, and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
His servants move him to his second chariot and bring him to Jerusalem, where he dies and is buried; “All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.” Arminian readers note the depth of the people’s grief.

2 Kings 23:30 also records his burial in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a nation mourning a king who had led them back to the LORD.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Josiah’s death marks the end of the last great reform before the exile.

verses.text: Jeremiah lamented for Josiah, and all the singing men and singing women spoke of Josiah in their lamentations to this day; and they made them an ordinance in Israel. Behold, they are written in the lamentations.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jeremiah lamented for Josiah,” and singers spoke of him in their lamentations; “they are written in the lamentations.” Arminian readers note Jeremiah’s grief for the king.

The collection named here is not necessarily the book of Lamentations; its identity is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the prophet mourning a faithful king.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Josiah’s death became an occasion of lasting lament in Israel.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Josiah and his good deeds, according to that which is written in the LORD’s law,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now the rest of the acts of Josiah and his good deeds, according to that which is written in the LORD’s law.” Arminian readers note that Josiah’s deeds are measured by God’s law.

The summary is warm toward him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Josiah’s goodness defined by faithfulness to Scripture.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Josiah is remembered for his obedience, despite his final decision.

verses.text: and his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The record of “his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.” Arminian readers note the reference to a fuller record.

The Chronicler regularly points to other sources.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the formula closing Josiah’s reign.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the reign of Judah’s last faithful king ends here, and the decline follows.
